summary: A glossary of terms specific to the Internet, written to help users understand the language they come across. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC is an alphabetical glossary of Internet terms and abbreviations. It helps readers look up vocabulary and follow references to related terms and sources.

subtitle: An alphabetical guide to Internet terms, abbreviations and related references.

tldr.problem: Internet users encounter specialized words and abbreviations, while general networking glossaries may not focus on terms specific to the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo arranges definitions alphabetically, provides cross-references, and credits sources for many entries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1983 is an Informational glossary, FYI 18, that obsoletes RFC 1392. Its definitions describe usage as recorded in August 1996.

today: RFC 1983 is an Informational memo from August 1996 that obsoletes RFC 1392. It is a historical snapshot of Internet terminology, not a current protocol specification.

sections.title: The Glossary's Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 1983 is FYI 18, an Informational glossary edited by G. Malkin. It focuses on terms specific to the Internet, while including basic terms and abbreviations that other entries use.

The User Glossary Working Group of the IETF User Services Area prepared the document. It replaces RFC 1392 and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo collects words used on the Internet and explains what they mean. It is a reference document, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: How to Use the Entries
sections.content:
Entries are arranged alphabetically, starting with non-letter items such as 10Base2, 802.x and the symbol :-). Some entries give a definition; others direct the reader to a main entry with “See” or to related entries with “See also”.

Many definitions identify their source with a bracketed reference tag, such as a cited RFC or another glossary. The reference list at the end supplies information about the cited sources.
sections.plainLanguage: Look up a word in alphabetical order. If an entry points elsewhere, follow that reference for the full definition or related terms.

sections.title: The Range of Topics
sections.content:
The entries cover hardware, protocols, organizations, services and Internet communication practices. Examples include 10Base2 and 10Base5 physical-layer specifications, Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), anonymous FTP, and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

The glossary also defines terms for the RFC series and FYI subseries. Its DNS entry lists top-level domains used at the time, including .COM, .EDU, .GOV and .MIL. These entries reflect the glossary's publication in August 1996.
sections.plainLanguage: The entries range from network equipment and protocols to organizations and online communication. The definitions describe the terminology as it was presented in 1996.

sections.title: Security Topics in a General Glossary
sections.content:
The RFC says that it does not explicitly discuss security. However, the glossary contains security-related entries, including access control, authentication, encryption, Kerberos, PGP, viruses and worms.

These entries explain terminology; they do not provide a security design or prescribe protection mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary is not a security guide. It defines some security terms that readers may encounter elsewhere.
